## 1. What the evidence actually is (and is not)

I have a single, global ranking of 1000 transcriptomic features by **mean |IG| attribution** from an MLP trained to predict input resistance (R_in). Critically, this ablation gives me: **magnitude only (no sign/direction), a population average (no per-cell or per-subtype structure), and no classifier-derived conditional logic**. The score distribution is also smooth and flat — the #1 feature (Fxyd6, 0.040) is only ~3× the #100 feature (0.013) and ~4× the #200 feature (0.010) — so no single gene dominates; the model's signal is distributed across many weakly contributing, likely co-expressed features. This means the ranking can *nominate* mechanisms but cannot *establish* them.

## 2. Patterns I can defend directly from the ranking

**(i) Plasmalemmal conductance genes are over-represented at the top.** By my rough count, ~14 of the top 100 features encode ion channels, electrogenic pumps/exchangers, or channel auxiliary subunits — Fxyd6 (#1, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase auxiliary subunit), Kcnq5 (#4, Kv7.5 M-current), Kcnmb4 (#7, BK-β4), Ano4 (#19, anoctamin-family anion channel), Kcna3 (#29, Kv1.3), Cacna2d3 (#41) and Cacna2d1 (#50, VGCC α2δ subunits), Atp2b4 (#45, PMCA), Gabrd (#61, GABA_A δ subunit), Htr3a (#62, 5-HT3A cation channel), Kcnd3 (#63, Kv4.3), Scn2b (#75), Dpp10 (#88, Kv4 accessory), Gabra4 (#98) — versus ~8% such genes across the full 1000. These are exactly the conductances that can be tonically active at rest, i.e., the only protein class that *directly* sets R_in = 1/g_rest.

**(ii) The machinery that gates those same conductances co-ranks.** Chrm3 (#97; muscarinic Gq signaling closes KCNQ/M-channels — the same current encoded by Kcnq5 at #4), Cnr1 (#38), Kctd16 (#236; GABA_B–GIRK coupling), Rgs6 (#68), Pde7b/Pde1a/Pde1c (#36/69/107), Adcy1 (#233), Orai2 (#164). Even post-transcriptional regulators of channel isoforms appear (Elavl2 #28, Srrm4 #103, Rbfox1 #190, Adarb2 #300). This coherence across the whole "resting-conductance regulatory stack" argues the model latched onto real membrane-conductance biology rather than random correlates.

**(iii) Cell-identity genes are prominent.** Dlx5/Dlx2/Dlx6 (#43/157/620), Lhx6 (#137), Bcl11b (#55), Tle4 (#10), Pvalb (#73), Htr3a (#62), Npy (#178), Penk (#80), Gad1 (#187), Nrgn (#9), Arpp21 (#48). A large share of the attribution therefore reflects *which interneuron subtype a cell is* — consistent with the known strong coupling of transcriptomic identity to electrophysiology in this exact dataset.

**(iv) An unanticipated glycosaminoglycan/ECM cluster** in the upper half: Ndst3 (#20), Extl1 (#110), Glce (#111), Csgalnact1 (#125), Chsy3 (#149), Ext1 (#177), B3gat2 (#352), Chst8 (#412), Hs3st2 (#472), plus Lama4 (#12), Crtac1 (#18), Col25a1 (#85), Hapln4 (#256). This could proxy perineuronal-net composition (PNNs preferentially enwrap PV+ cells) and/or cell size/surface area — both correlate with R_in — but this reading is speculative.

**(v) Notable absences/asymmetries:** no Hcn genes appear anywhere in the 1000-feature list (Ih is a well-established R_in determinant, so conclusions are conditional on this feature space), and canonical markers Vip (#714), Sst (#744), Gad2 (#896) rank *low* while Pvalb ranks mid — likely because attribution is spread across each subtype's co-expression module, a caution that rank order ≠ importance of the underlying biological process.

## 3. Rationale

R_in is the inverse of total resting membrane conductance. The ranking is consistent with a two-layer scheme: **upstream**, subtype-identity transcriptional programs (Dlx, Lhx6, Bcl11b, Tle4) specify a membrane-protein repertoire; **downstream**, the tonically active fraction of that repertoire — KCNQ5 M-current, Kv1.3, Kv4.3, K2P leak, SK2, GIRK2, GABA_A(GABRD), Ca²⁺-activated anion conductances (ANO4), and the FXYD6-modulated Na⁺/K⁺ pump — sets g_rest and hence R_in. The co-ranking of the receptors and second-messenger components that gate these same conductances supports this reading.

## 4. Single best hypothesis

**Input resistance across mouse cortical GABAergic interneurons is set primarily by a cell-type-specified "resting-conductance module" — anchored by the KCNQ5/Kv7.5 M-current (Kcnq5, #4), with Kv1.3, Kv4.3–KChIP4, K2P leak (Kcnk2/3), SK2, GIRK2 and BK-β4 as secondary contributors — acting together with a GABRD-dependent tonic GABA_A shunt (#61) and an FXYD6-modulated Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase current (#1); cells expressing this module more strongly should have *lower* input resistance (direction inferred from biophysics, not from the data).**

## 5. Discriminating, testable predictions

1. A module expression score correlates with measured R_in (negatively for the K⁺ components). Crucially, a **within-subtype** correlation would support causal effector status; a purely **between-subtype** correlation would indicate identity proxy — this is precisely the analysis the omitted classifier stage would have enabled.
2. XE991/linopirdine (KCNQ blockers) increases R_in by an amount proportional to Kcnq5 expression (patch-seq or FISH-guided patching); retigabine does the opposite.
3. Dendrotoxin-K shifts R_in preferentially in Kcna3-high cells; gabazine-sensitive tonic holding current scales with Gabrd.
4. Ouabain-sensitive pump current scales with Fxyd6 expression (FXYD6's electrophysiological role is, to my knowledge, untested — a genuinely novel candidate).
5. (Speculative) PNN/GAG manipulation (e.g., chondroitinase ABC) alters R_in in the corresponding subtype.

## 6. (a) or (b)?

At the level of principle this **confirms established knowledge (a)**: subthreshold K⁺ conductances (M-current, leak) and tonic GABA_A inhibition set R_in, and transcriptomic identity predicts electrophysiology in this dataset. At the level of the specific gene nominations — KCNQ5 as the leading channel correlate of interneuron R_in, FXYD6/pump current, the GAG-synthesis cluster — it **proposes new testable mechanisms (b)**. Supporting literature (from memory; verify before formal use): Brown & Adams, 1980, *Nature* (M-current); Delmas & Brown, 2005, *Nat Rev Neurosci* (KCNQ modulation); Stell et al., 2003, *PNAS* (δ-subunit tonic inhibition); Sweadner & Rael, 2000, *Genomics* (FXYD proteins as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase regulators); Anderson et al., 1997, *Science* (Dlx genes and interneuron development); Gouwens et al., 2020, *Cell* (this dataset); Scala et al., 2021, *Nat Neurosci*; Cadwell et al., 2016, *Nat Biotechnol* (patch-seq gene–ephys associations); Toledo-Rodriguez et al., 2004 (channel mRNA–ephys correlations in neocortical interneurons).

## 7. What this evidence cannot establish (honest limits)

- **No direction of effect** — the sign of every relationship above is inferred from biophysics, not data.
- **Effector vs. identity proxy is unresolvable** from a global mean-|IG| ranking; the classifier/subgroup stage that was deliberately omitted here is exactly what would resolve it.
- **Attribution is non-unique under co-expression** — high ranks may reflect module membership rather than causality.
- Several top genes have **no known electrophysiological role** (Pcdh8 #2, Coro6 #3, Cpne7 #5, Fam19a2 #6, Rell1 #11, Tmem145 #13, Flt3 #14, plus unannotated RIKEN/LOC loci); I will not invent mechanisms for them — they likely ride along with subtype identity/morphology or model idiosyncrasies I cannot diagnose from this list.
- **No model performance, stability, or per-cell statistics** were provided, and canonical excitatory markers (Cux2 #145, Rorb #621, Tbr1 #808, Fezf2 #814, Satb2 #180) appear in a nominally GABAergic dataset, which I cannot interpret without expression distributions.

**Bottom line:** the IG-only ranking is sufficient to nominate a specific, coherent, testable hypothesis (a KCNQ5-anchored resting-conductance module with GABRD and FXYD6 components, deployed per subtype), but it is not sufficient to establish direction, causality, or subtype-specificity. My confidence in the hypothesis as stated is therefore low-to-moderate.
